faqs.q: What is the base annual salary for a qualified Sydney Trains driver?
faqs.a: Under the Sydney Trains and NSW TrainLink Enterprise Agreement, a qualified driver (thereafter classification) receives $1,959.60 per week including the industry allowance, which works out to $101,899 per year. This is the base rate before shift penalties, overtime, and allowances.

faqs.q: How do I convert a train driver's hourly rate to an annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply the hourly rate by the number of ordinary hours per week (usually 38) and then by 52 weeks. For example, a driver earning $48.98 per hour (the 2026 rate for a 2nd year driver) would have an annual base of $48.98 × 38 × 52 = $96,784.48. The enterprise agreement publishes weekly rates that already include the industry allowance, so you can also multiply the weekly rate by 52.

faqs.q: Do train drivers earn more than the base rate shown in the agreement?
faqs.a: Yes, most drivers earn significantly more because of shift penalties, weekend rates, and overtime. The base rate is the minimum; actual take-home pay is often 20–30% higher. The enterprise agreement sets separate allowances for afternoon, night, and early morning shifts, and overtime is paid at time-and-a-half or double time.

bodyMarkdown:
## Train Driver Salary Sydney: Understanding the Base Rates

If you are researching a **train driver salary Sydney**, the most reliable figures come from the enterprise agreement that covers Sydney Trains and NSW TrainLink. These rates are set by the Fair Work Commission and are the legal minimums for the classifications they cover. This article explains how to convert those base rates into annual and fortnightly figures, and what factors push actual earnings higher.

### How the Annual Salary Is Calculated

The standard formula for converting an hourly rate to an annual salary is:

**Hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

For full-time transport workers, ordinary hours are 38 per week (76 per fortnight). So if you know the hourly rate, you multiply by 38 and then by 52. The enterprise agreement often publishes weekly rates that include an industry allowance, making the conversion even simpler: just multiply the weekly rate by 52.

For example, a qualified Sydney Trains driver (the "Thereafter" classification) has a weekly base rate of $1,959.60 including the industry allowance from 1 July 2026. That gives an annual base of $101,899.20, as shown in the pay schedules.

### Train Driver Base Rates Under the Enterprise Agreement

The Sydney Trains and NSW TrainLink Enterprise Agreement (AE529763) sets out pay rates for drivers, guards, and other train crew. The rates increase each year; from 1 July 2026, the key driver classifications are:

- **1st Year Trainee:** $1,797.30 per week ($93,460 per year)
- **1st Year Competent:** $1,833.05 per week ($95,319 per year)
- **2nd Year:** $1,916.95 per week ($99,681 per year)
- **Thereafter (qualified):** $1,959.60 per week ($101,899 per year)
- **Driver Trainer:** $2,180.45 per week ($113,383 per year)
- **Principal Driver:** $2,255.30 per week ($117,276 per year)

These figures include the industry allowance, which is a weekly amount added to the base hourly rate. The agreement also lists rates without the allowance; the inclusive rate is the one used for annual salary calculations.

For comparison, a qualified Metro Trains Melbourne driver earns $135,657 per year base, reflecting different enterprise agreements and cost structures.

### What Affects Take-Home Pay

The base rates above are the minimum. Most train drivers work rotating rosters that attract significant penalties:

- **Afternoon shift allowance:** $5.03 per hour for drivers and guards
- **Night shift allowance:** $5.92 per hour
- **Early morning shift allowance:** $5.03 per hour
- **Overtime:** Paid at time-and-a-half for the first two hours and double time thereafter
- **Weekend penalties:** Saturday work attracts a loading, Sunday work is often double time

These penalties can add 20–40% to the base rate. A driver earning $101,899 base might take home $120,000–$130,000 before tax. The enterprise agreement states that where multiple penalties apply, only the single most advantageous penalty is paid—they do not stack.

### Comparing to Other Benchmarks

The National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. A qualified train driver's base rate of about $48.98 per hour (for a 2nd year driver) is well above the minimum, reflecting the skilled nature of the role and the responsibility for passenger safety.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, average weekly earnings for full-time adult employees in May 2026 were $2,083.70 (ordinary time). A Sydney Trains driver's base weekly rate of $1,959.60 is slightly below that average, but once penalties are added, many drivers exceed the average.

### Using the Timesheet Calculator

To estimate your own annual salary from an hourly rate, use [the timesheet](/). Enter your base hourly rate (without casual loading) and the calculator will show the annual, fortnightly, and weekly figures. If you are a casual employee, check the 25% casual loading box—the calculator adds it on top. Remember that superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings at 12% (up to the $270,830 maximum contribution base).

For more detailed breakdowns of award rates and enterprise agreements, see the [job pay](/topics/job-pay) page. You can also explore [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) for other occupations.

### Important Notes on the Estimates

- Annual pay is calculated as hourly rate × 38 hours × 52 weeks, assuming no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, and no salary sacrifice.
- Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings, paid on top, and stops at the maximum contribution base.
- Tax uses the 2026–27 resident rates: nil up to $18,200, 15% to $45,000, 30% to $135,000, 37% to $190,000, and 45% above that. Medicare levy is generally 2%.
- These are estimates, not a determination of your actual pay or tax obligations.
